46: | Per-decision **`persona_parameters` with mythic names** (Sekhmet, Brigid, …) | **M2 hazard.** Use **`slot_ref` keys** (`P1`…`P10`, `GRAND_OVERSIGHT`) or omit until overlay resolution exists. Defaults live in WAD meditate config, not engine. |
47: | Full Structured MADR **audit / technologies / audience** | Optional tags only. Do not block parse. |
48: | **DEBATE replay retrospective** fields | T5 only. Empty `retrospective: null` is enough. |
49: 
50: ### 1.3 Missing fields (add in T0)
51: 
52: ```yaml
53: schema_version: 1          # required — enables future forbid-safe evolution
54: id: D1                     # stable decision id
55: title: "..."
56: status: proposed           # see state machine
57: created: 2026-07-18
58: updated: 2026-07-18
59: authority: human_review
60: decision_by: null          # optional ISO date
61: meditate_ready: false
62: category: architecture     # free string or small enum
63: tags: []
64: drivers:
65:   primary: "..."
66:   secondary: []
67: options: []
68: relationships: []
69: # Decision outcome (set only on accept path / superseding record)
70: chosen_option: null        # option id
71: decided_at: null
72: decided_by: null           # agent_id or "human"
73: rationale: null            # short string
74: supersedes: null
75: superseded_by: null
76: evidence_refs: []          # paths / handoff ids / commits — cheap provenance
77: ```
78: 
79: **JSON Schema**: yes for CI/`decide` validation. Keep **one** schema file under e.g. `config/schemas/decision_v1.json` (or `docs/decisions/schema/`) and load via existing config patterns — not a second YAML dialect.
80: 
81: ### 1.4 Status machine
82: 
83: Correct **logical** machine:
84: 
85: ```
86: proposed ──► accepted
87:     │            │
88:     │            └──► superseded   (only via NEW record that supersedes this id)
89:     └──► deprecated                (rare; no successor)
90: ```
91: 
92: **Implementation nuance (ADR purity vs git reality):**
93: 
94: - Golden rule: **do not rewrite accepted decision body** (options, drivers, rationale of the past).
95: - **Allowed mutation on the superseded record**: set `status: superseded`, `superseded_by: D24`, `updated:` only — or keep original immutable and express supersession **only** on the new file + an index.  
96:   **Recommend for T0**: allow a **minimal status patch** on the old file (status + superseded_by + updated). Reject any other field changes on non-`proposed` records.
97: 
98: Do **not** “move file from `open/` to `decided/`” as the primary mechanism if it breaks stable paths and git blame. Prefer:
99: 
100: ```
101: docs/decisions/catalog/D001.yaml   # stable path for life of id
102: ```
103: 
104: Optional index: `docs/decisions/INDEX.yaml` regenerated by `list` (not hand-edited).
105: 
106: ### 1.5 Schema score
107: 
108: | Dimension | Score | Note |
109: |-----------|-------|------|
110: | ADR alignment | High | Good |
111: | Agent fit | Medium-High | After cutting MAD + mythic keys |
112: | Complexity vs T0 | Currently high | Needs pruning |
113: | Security / forbid | Good if versioned | Follow WadManifest V2 pattern |
114: 
115: **Answer to Kali’s criteria question:** weighted criteria are **not required for v1**. Keep optional. Consensus can be `chosen_option` + free-text `rationale`.
116: 
117: **Authority field:** **keep** — CLI should branch on it; do not hide auth only in flags.
118: 
119: **Deadlines:** **keep optional on the record**; graph need not compute them.

122: 
123: ## 2. Architecture review
124: 
125: ### 2.1 DecisionEngine abstraction
126: 
127: | Question | Recommendation |
128: |----------|----------------|
129: | Class vs module | Thin **`DecisionStore` / `DecisionEngine`** class is fine — mirrors `EntityRegistry` style. Avoid god-object. |
130: | Location | **`src/omega/governance/decisions.py`** (or `src/omega/decisions/`) inside the monorepo. **Not** a separate PyPI package for T0. |
131: | Package boundary | CLI in `src/omega/cli/decision_cli.py` + `app.add_typer(..., name="decision")` next to `youtube` / `bundle`. |
132: | Data plane | **Git-tracked YAML under `docs/decisions/catalog/`** is correct for ADRs (reviewable, pushable). Runtime state does **not** belong in SQLite for T0. |
133: 
134: ### 2.2 CRUD + supersession
135: 
136: Sound design if:
137: 
138: 1. **`create` / `update`** only while `status == proposed` (full body edits).
139: 2. **`accept` / `decide`**:
140:    - writes **new** file `D{n+1}` with `supersedes: D{old}`, `status: accepted`, `chosen_option`, …
141:    - patches old: `status: superseded`, `superseded_by: D{n+1}` (minimal).
142: 3. **Never** overwrite accepted option text.
143: 
144: Naming: prefer **zero-padded ids** (`D001`) for sort stability once count > 9.
145: 
146: ### 2.3 Atomic writes & concurrency
147: 
148: - **`write tmp → os.replace`** (or existing `batch_writer` pattern): **required**.
149: - **Concurrent multi-agent writes**: real risk on HMC. T0 options (pick one, document):
150:   1. **Convention**: only Kali (or single `decider` agent_id) runs `decide` — enforce in CLI via env/`authority` + optional allowlist.
151:   2. **Advisory lock file** `docs/decisions/.lock` with TTL (file-based, AnyIO-friendly).
152:   3. **Defer flock/sqlite** until pain (aligns with “build from pain”).
153: 
154: **Do not** invent Redis locks for decisions.
155: 
156: ### 2.4 Cache
157: 
158: - **T0: always read from disk** for `list`/`show`/`decide`. 23–50 YAML files is nothing.
159: - In-memory graph cache only if profiling says so (T1-graph+). Invalidate on any write.
160: 
161: ### 2.5 Engine-stack firewall (M2)
162: 
163: Critical:
164: 
165: - Decision tooling in `src/omega/` must **not** import ANAi entity names or WAD-specific myth.
166: - MEDITATE scaffold must resolve **slots → lenses via active IWAD**, same as `meditate/lens_registry.py` direction.
167: - Catalog content (D1 text about Sekhmet) may mention myth; **engine code must not**.
168: 
169: ### 2.6 Architecture score
170: 
171: | Dimension | Score | Note |
172: |-----------|-------|------|
173: | Fit with monorepo | High | Typer CLI pattern already exists |
174: | Crash safety | High if atomic | Standard |
175: | Multi-agent safety | Medium | Needs explicit single-writer policy |
176: | M2 safety | Medium | Fix persona key design |
177:

179: 
180: ## 3. CLI review
181: 
182: ### 3.1 Namespace
183: 
184: **`omega decision …` is correct.**
185: 
186: - Matches existing sub-apps (`youtube`, `bundle`).
187: - `omega adr` is jargon-heavy for agents; `omega decide` collides with verb vs noun group.
188: - Keep noun group: `decision list|show|decide|graph`.
189: 
190: ### 3.2 Commands (T0+T1-core)
191: 
192: | Command | Required T0? | Notes |
193: |---------|--------------|--------|
194: | `list` | Yes | Filters: `--status`, `--tag`, `--overdue`, `--meditate-ready` |
195: | `show ID` | Yes | Print YAML + **supersession chain** (walk `supersedes` / `superseded_by`) |
196: | `decide ID --option OPT` | Yes | Creates successor; optional `--rationale`; **`--human-confirmed` only when `authority` ∈ {human, human_review}** |
197: | `graph` | T1-graph | ASCII only; `--focus`, `--depth`; plain text default (agent-safe) |
198: | `validate` | Nice 30-min add | Run JSON Schema over catalog — high ROI for migration |
199: 
200: ### 3.3 Flags & UX
201: 
202: - **`--human-confirmed`**: **not always**. Gate by `authority`. For `agent` authority, log `decided_by=agent_id` from Hivemind/env.
203: - **Color**: Rich tables OK for humans; **`--plain`** for handoff paste / CI.
204: - **Exit codes**: non-zero on validation failure, unknown id, missing human confirm — agents need this.
205: - **Idempotency**: `decide` on already-accepted id should **error** (force explicit supersede of latest head).
206: 
207: ### 3.4 CLI score
208: 
209: Design is clean and adr-tools-evolved. Main fix: **authority-aware confirm**, not blanket flag.
210: 
211: ---
212: 
213: ## 4. MEDITATE integration review
214: 
215: ### 4.1 Are BE uptake/anchoring parameters meaningful in single-inference MEDITATE?
216: 
217: **Partially — with caveats. Risk of cargo-cult is real.**
218: 
219: Belief Engine’s `u` / `a` are **controls on iterative log-odds updates across evidence steps**. A **single** oracle call that role-plays 10 personas does **not** run that loop unless you:
220: 
221: 1. structure the prompt into explicit Extract→Judge→Update stages, **and**
222: 2. either multi-call or force the model to emit intermediate belief states.
223: 
224: What **is** still useful in T1-scaffold:
225: 
226: - **Named stance biases** as *prompt annotations* (“P1: high anchoring on hardware constraints”) — qualitative, not numerical magic.
227: - **Reproducibility**: same decision file → same scaffold text → better audit than free-form chat.
228: - **Separation**: deliberation config lives with the decision, not in agent memory soup.
229: 
230: What is **not** honest for T1:
231: 
232: - Claiming numerical `uptake: 0.4` is a calibrated BE parameter without multi-step update + measurement.
233: - Hardcoding ANAi persona tables in core.
234: 
235: ### 4.2 Where should parameters live?
236: 
237: | Layer | Owns |
238: |-------|------|
239: | WAD meditate lenses / overlay | Default stance hints per **slot** |
240: | Decision file | Optional **overrides** for this question only |
241: | Engine | Template renderer only — no mythic defaults |
242: 
243: ### 4.3 5-step BE loop inside one oracle call?
244: 
245: **Implementable as prompt structure, not as real BE.** Ship T1-scaffold as:
246: 
247: ```
248: omega decision meditate-scaffold D1   # or: omega meditate --decision D1 --scaffold-only
249: → writes / prints prompt markdown
250: → human or agent runs inference separately
251: ```
252: 
253: **Do not** auto-call the model inside T0/T1 unless you already have a stable meditate path and budget for flakes.
254: 
255: ### 4.4 MEDITATE score
256: 
257: | Item | Recommendation |
258: |------|----------------|
259: | T1-scaffold in 7h sprint | **Optional / cut first** if schedule slips |
260: | Numeric u/a in YAML | **Defer to T2** or store as optional opaque map with no engine math |
261: | Slot-keyed hints | **Yes** |
262: | Full automated MEDITATE | **T2**, pain-triggered |

14: ## 0. HEADLINE FINDING
15: 
16: The dual-review produced a genuinely useful result — and it's a *more* interesting result than first reported. The two reviewers did not work from the same materials or the same access model: Web Claude worked entirely from a curated, web-delivered context pack (eight XML bundles, no live repository access), while Grok CLI worked as a local agent with direct filesystem access to the actual `docs/`, `src/`, and `tests/` trees, plus its own prior research artifacts already on disk. Despite that asymmetry, the two reviews converged on nearly every load-bearing conclusion (§2). That convergence is a stronger signal than same-input convergence would have been — it means the curated context pack captured enough of what mattered that a web-only reviewer without repo access reasoned its way to the same place as a reviewer who could `grep` the actual codebase. That's a real, if informal, validation of the Context Pack tool's curation quality, and it's the headline finding of this revision. The exercise also surfaced concrete protocol defects (§5), the most consequential being a version-control gap in the handoff documents themselves (§1.1, §5.1) — fixable before the next round.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. WHAT WAS ACTUALLY COMPARED
21: 
22: Both reviewers were asked to produce the same seven sections (schema, architecture, CLI, MEDITATE integration, scope/effort, risks, verdict), and neither had access to the other's output while writing — the review was genuinely parallel, not sequential, which matters for what follows. **That is where the symmetry ends.** The materials and access each reviewer actually had were substantially different, detailed in §1.1.
23: 
24: ### 1.1 Correction: The Two Reviewers Did Not Have Comparable Inputs
25: 
26: This report's first draft assumed Grok CLI worked from the same eight-bundle context pack (`00_PROJECT_MANIFEST.md` + 7 XML bundles) that Web Claude did. That was wrong. Two distinct handoff documents exist for the same Hivemind packet id (`ho_749ed27155cd`):
27: 
28: | | Web Claude's handoff | Grok CLI's actual handoff |
29: |---|---|---|
30: | Document | `handoff.xml` bundle (embedding `KALI_TO_GROK_CLI_DECISION_TOOLS_REVIEW_20260719.md`) | `KALI_TO_GROK_CLI_DECISION_WORKSPACE_HANDOFF_20260719.md` (uploaded this turn) |
31: | Stated scope | Narrow — tools implementation only. Opens by explicitly *cancelling* a prior broader ask: "Previous handoff was incorrect... those decisions are internal engine questions, irrelevant to external review." | Broad — ratify all 23 open decisions, validate the grounded meditation, deliver a binding verdict on D-297, review the Sovereign Exit Protocol, evaluate T2–T5 trigger conditions, all in addition to the tools implementation review |
32: | Required reading | 8 curated XML bundles, ~44K tokens, assembled and shipped to a web session with no filesystem access | 5+ full source documents (438, 404, 388, 369, 261 lines) plus reference reading, all read directly off disk by an agent with native repo access |
33: | Access model | Web-only: whatever was packed, plus live web search | Local CLI: full read access to `docs/`, `src/`, `tests/`, `data/coordination/`, its own prior research files already on disk |
34: 
35: **The two handoffs are not the same document, and it is not clear from the artifacts available to Web Claude which one Grok CLI actually executed against, or when/how the correction from broad to narrow scope reached it.** Grok's delivered review (`GROK_CLI_DECISION_TOOLS_REVIEW_20260719.md`) explicitly states its scope as narrow — "Out of scope: D1–D23 content, D-297 substance, Jem gaps, Sovereign Exit" — matching the *corrected*, narrow handoff almost verbatim, not the broad one uploaded this turn. Two explanations are consistent with the evidence: either the corrected handoff (`handoff.xml`'s content) reached Grok through Hivemind after the broad one and superseded it in Grok's working context, or Grok — with native repo access — independently discovered the scope contradiction by reading both handoff documents on disk and self-resolved toward the narrower one. Web Claude cannot distinguish between these from the materials available, and flags this as an open question for Kali rather than guessing. Either way, it means Grok's review was produced against a *richer and differently-scoped* information environment than Web Claude's, not an identical one.
36: 
37: **Why this strengthens rather than weakens the convergence finding in §2**: same-input convergence between two reviewers is a moderate signal — it mostly tells you the design is legible enough that careful readers reach the same conclusion. *Different*-input convergence, where one reviewer had live repository access and a 100+-line broader mandate while the other had only a curated 44K-token pack and web search, is a stronger signal, because it rules out "they agreed because they were shown the same thing" as the explanation. The two reviews agreed despite reasoning from different vantage points with different completeness of information — which is closer to genuine independent validation than the original framing gave credit for. It also means the curated context pack — the thing under the user's direct control and the one artifact in this pipeline that isn't native tool access — did enough work that its absence of repo access didn't produce a materially worse review. That is a meaningful data point in favor of continuing to invest in pack curation quality as a lower-cost substitute for full repo access, at least for architecture-level review tasks of this shape.
38: 
39: **One factual correction that still stands from v1.0**: the pack's own manifest describes `handoff.xml` as containing "Grok CLI's CONDITIONAL GO review (410 lines)." It does not — `handoff.xml` contains Kali's *request to* Grok CLI, not Grok's answer. This is now understood to be compounded by the broader version-churn issue above: there were at least two handoff documents in circulation for the same packet id, and the pack's manifest mislabeled a third thing (a request document) as if it were Grok's output. See §5.1.

49: | Overall verdict | go-with-conditions | CONDITIONAL GO |
50: | Is `persona_parameters` with mythic names an M2 violation? | Yes — reject, use `slot_ref` | Yes — "M2 hazard," use `slot_ref` |
51: | Is the 7h estimate realistic? | No — ~9h | No — 9–11h |
52: | Should the 23-decision migration be its own PR? | Yes, two-PR split | Yes, two-PR split, identical reasoning |
53: | Should `criteria` weighted scoring be required? | No — optional | No — optional |
54: | Are numeric Belief-Engine `uptake`/`anchoring` parameters meaningful in single-inference MEDITATE? | No — cargo-cult without an iterative loop; static template only | No — same diagnosis, same fix |
55: | What CLI namespace? | `omega decision {list,show,decide,graph}` | Same; explicitly rejects `omega adr`/`omega decide` as jargon/verb-noun collision |
56: | Atomic write pattern? | `tempfile` + `fsync` + `os.replace` | "write tmp → os.replace... required" |
57: 
58: **Why this matters more than either review alone — and more than the original framing gave it credit for**: this was not two reviewers looking at the same page and agreeing. Per §1.1, Web Claude reasoned from a curated 44K-token pack with no repository access; Grok CLI reasoned as a local agent with direct filesystem access to the full source tree and a broader initial mandate. That two reviewers with different architectures, different tool access, and — critically — different *completeness of information* landed on the same technical conclusions is a materially stronger validity check than same-input agreement would have been. It also means the gap between "curated pack + web search" and "native repo access" was, for this review task, small enough not to change the outcome — which is the closest thing to an empirical read this project has on whether the Context Pack tool's curation is doing its job. When two independent reviews converge under these conditions, treat the shared conclusion as settled and stop spending further review cycles re-litigating it — the marginal value of a third opinion on an already-converged point is low. Route further scrutiny toward the points where they *didn't* converge (§3) or where one caught something the other missed (§4).
59: 
60: ---
61: 
62: ## 3. DIVERGENCE ANALYSIS
63: 
64: Only one substantive disagreement surfaced, and it's a legitimate design-taste question, not an error on either side:
65: 
66: **File format**: Web Claude recommended YAML frontmatter + Markdown body (`D0001.md`), citing that this is literally what `structured-madr` (the precedent both reviews cite as the schema's lineage) actually uses. Grok recommended pure YAML (`D001.yaml`), citing consistency with the project's existing config-file culture (`entities.yaml`, `lenses.yaml`).
67: 
68: Neither is wrong. This is worth noting as a *category* of divergence distinct from disagreement: both reviewers were reasoning correctly from different but equally valid precedents. Both precedents were visible in Web Claude's pack too (the `entities.yaml`/`lenses.yaml` convention appears in `implementation.xml`), so this split isn't simply explained by Grok having repo access Web Claude lacked — it's a genuine judgment call where the pack itself doesn't adjudicate which precedent should win when two exist. **This is a gap in the source material, not a gap in either reviewer, and not an artifact of the access asymmetry in §1.1.** When a context pack (or a repo) contains multiple legitimate precedents that point different directions on a low-stakes question, expect reviewers to split on it regardless of how much they can see, and don't read the split as either reviewer being wrong.
69: 
70: The lighter divergence — Web Claude specified `portalocker.Lock()` as the concrete concurrency mechanism, Grok named three options and said "pick one, document it" — isn't really a disagreement either; Grok's structure is the decision space, Web Claude's is a specific point inside it. Worth noting for §6: asking reviewers explicitly whether they should commit to one implementation or enumerate the option space would resolve this kind of non-disagreement before it looks like one.
71: 
72: ---
73: 
74: ## 4. ASYMMETRIC CATCHES — WHAT EACH REVIEWER FOUND ALONE
75: 
76: This is the actual value-add of running two reviews instead of one. Neither review was complete on its own; together they cover more ground than either would have separately.
77: 
78: ### 4.1 Grok caught, Web Claude missed
79: 
80: - **Idempotency bug**: Web Claude's original `decide()` sketch only rejected `status == "superseded"`. It would have silently allowed re-deciding an *already-accepted* record, producing two competing "accepted" successors for the same question. Grok's decide-algorithm sketch explicitly required "reject if status ≠ proposed (or ≠ head of chain)" — a correctness bug in Web Claude's code that Grok's more algorithmic, step-by-step spec style caught and Web Claude's narrative-prose style did not.
81: - **ID-allocator race condition**: Grok's risk list flagged "id collision without allocator" as a secondary risk in one line, without a mitigation. Web Claude had not addressed id allocation at all in the first draft — `_next_id()` was hand-waved. Grok's one-line flag was enough to prompt Web Claude to specify a proper fix (separate lock scoped to the allocator step) once cross-referenced.
82: - **`validate` as a standalone command**: Grok proposed a ~30-minute `omega decision validate` command as a "nice add," specifically because it's the highest-ROI tool for catching malformed files *during* the 23-decision migration rather than after. Web Claude had validation logic embedded inside `create`/`decide` but hadn't surfaced it as an independently callable command — a real usability gap for the migration phase specifically.
83: - **`decided_by` / `rationale` fields**: Grok's field list distinguished "who proposed this" from "who executed the accept" and added a scannable one-line rationale separate from the full narrative body. Web Claude's schema had `proposer` but conflated authorship and execution.
84: - **Relationship-cycle detection**: Grok's risk list flagged "relationship cycles in graph without cycle detection" as a secondary risk. Web Claude's `graph` command spec had no cycle handling at all until this was folded in.
85: 
86: ### 4.2 Web Claude added, beyond what Grok's review covered
87: 
88: - **Live technical verification via web search**: Web Claude ran targeted searches during the *implementation manual* pass (not the review pass) and surfaced that the `atomicwrites` PyPI package — a natural first reach for "atomic file writes in Python" — was archived by its own maintainer in 2022 and formally deprecated from downstream package repositories in 2025, with upstream explicitly recommending `os.replace`/`os.rename` instead. Neither review's initial pass caught this; it only surfaced because Web Claude went one level deeper than "review the design" into "verify the exact library choice a builder would reach for by default." This is a category of catch that requires tool access (web search) rather than architectural reasoning — worth noting for §5.3.
89: - **Concrete library selection with version/maintenance status**: `portalocker` (current major version 3.x, actively maintained, explicitly cross-platform) named specifically, with the reasoning for why hand-rolled `fcntl`/`msvcrt` branching is worse. Grok's review correctly identified the *need* for locking but left the library choice as "pick one, document it" — a reasonable scope call for an architecture review, but it means the actual implementation manual still had to do that research separately.
90: - **Exact JSON Schema draft and conditional-validation mechanism**: confirmed `Draft202012Validator` is current and that `if/then` blocks are the correct 2020-12 mechanism for "require `chosen_option` only when `status: accepted`" — a level of API-specific detail below what either review's architecture-level pass covered, again only reachable via direct doc lookup.
91: 
92: **Pattern**: Grok's catches were almost entirely *logical/architectural* — gaps found by simulating the algorithm step-by-step. Web Claude's additions beyond convergence were almost entirely *empirical* — facts about the current state of specific libraries that no amount of architectural reasoning alone would surface, only checkable by looking. Neither mode is superior; they're complementary, and a review protocol that only requests one of them will systematically miss the other's class of error. See §6.
93: 
94: ---
95: 
96: ## 5. PROTOCOL FINDINGS — WHAT TO FIX BEFORE THE NEXT DUAL REVIEW
97: 
98: ### 5.1 Context pack manifest labeling is a real defect, not a cosmetic one
99: 
100: `00_PROJECT_MANIFEST.md` and the `handoff.xml` bundle description both assert that `handoff.xml` contains Grok's completed review. It contains Kali's request *to* Grok. This is the kind of error that, in a less careful reviewer, propagates silently: a reviewer told "synthesize your findings against Grok's CONDITIONAL GO review in `handoff.xml`" who doesn't actually check the bundle content against the claim will produce a synthesis section that's fabricated — citing "Grok found X" when X was never in the document it read. Web Claude avoided this only because the actual content of the bundle (a request document, addressed "Kali → Grok CLI," full of open questions rather than answers) was obviously inconsistent with the claimed content, and said so rather than papering over it.
101: 
102: **Fix**: whatever process generates context-pack manifests should validate that a bundle's stated `purpose` matches its actual content before the pack ships to a reviewer — even a simple check (does the file described as "Grok's review" contain the string "Verdict" or "CONDITIONAL GO" anywhere?) would have caught this. More generally: **a reviewer that silently trusts a manifest's description of a bundle's contents, instead of verifying it, is a liability.** Consider adding an explicit instruction to future review-handoff prompts: "Verify that each bundle's actual content matches its stated purpose before using it; flag any mismatch rather than proceeding on the stated description."
103: 
104: ### 5.2 What the review-request design got right (keep doing this)
105: 
106: - **Explicit scope guardrails** ("do NOT review the 23 content decisions") were honored by both reviewers without drift. Neither review wandered into ratifying D1–D23. This is worth crediting to the handoff design, not assuming it happens by default — scope drift is a common failure mode in open-ended review requests, and it didn't happen here.
107: - **Mandated output sections** (schema / architecture / CLI / MEDITATE / scope-effort / risks / verdict) produced two reviews that are structurally comparable line-for-line, which is what made §2–§4 of this report possible to write at all. If the two reviews had used different organizing structures, cross-referencing them would have taken considerably longer and been much more error-prone. **A rigid required-sections template is doing real work here — don't relax it for future reviews in the name of "letting the reviewer use their judgment on structure."**
108: - **Verification criteria embedded in the request** (e.g., "all 23 catalog entries parse cleanly," "no mythic persona names in engine defaults") gave both reviewers a shared, falsifiable bar rather than a vague "is this good" prompt. Both reviews' outputs are answerable against those criteria directly. Keep authoring review requests with explicit, checkable acceptance criteria per section, not just open questions.
109: 
110: ### 5.3 Neither review request explicitly asked for empirical verification — and it should have
111: 
112: Nothing in the review-request system prompt told either reviewer to check current library status, API signatures, or package maintenance state. Web Claude did this anyway (§4.2) because it has web search available and treats architecture reviews involving specific technology choices as warranting it. But this wasn't *requested* — it was a judgment call, and a differently-tuned instance might not have made it. Given that the empirical catches in §4.2 (a deprecated package that's still the natural first search result for "atomic writes Python") are exactly the kind of error that silently ships and then breaks in production six months later, this should not be left to individual reviewer judgment.
113: 
114: **Fix**: for any future review request touching specific library/tool/API choices, add an explicit line: *"Where the design specifies or implies a particular library, package, or API, verify its current maintenance status and correct usage via web search before endorsing it — do not rely on training-data familiarity alone."* This converts an optional judgment call into a protocol requirement, closing the exact gap this exercise happened to catch by luck of which reviewer had search available and used it.
115: 
116: ### 5.4 There was no standing mechanism for synthesizing parallel reviews — this report is ad hoc
117: 
118: The dual review happened, produced two good independent documents, and then sat as two separate files until the user manually asked for a synthesis. Nothing in the process automatically triggers a cross-review synthesis step, and nothing defines what that synthesis should contain. This report itself is the template for what that step should produce, but it was requested reactively rather than being a defined stage of the review protocol.
119: 
120: **Fix**: when a decision or design goes through parallel review (which should happen for architecture-level questions — see §6), make the synthesis step a **defined, mandatory third stage**, not an optional follow-up: (1) Reviewer A works independently, (2) Reviewer B works independently with no access to A's output, (3) a synthesis pass — by either reviewer, a third agent, or Kali directly — produces exactly the kind of convergence/divergence/asymmetric-catch breakdown in §2–§4 of this report, using a fixed template. Once the Decision Workspace tooling from this sprint exists, this synthesis step is a natural candidate for its own `evidence_refs`-linked decision record: "D-XXX: Parallel review synthesis is a mandatory third stage for architecture-level decisions."
121: 
122: ### 5.5 Reviewers didn't know a parallel review existed — sequencing should be explicit
123: 
124: Web Claude's first pass proceeded as if it were the only review happening (reasonably, since the mislabeled `handoff.xml` didn't reveal that Grok's review existed or was concurrent). Had Web Claude known a second, independent review was running in parallel with the same scope, it might have made different choices about where to spend depth — for instance, leaning harder into the empirical/web-search mode (§4.2) precisely because that's the mode less likely to be duplicated by an architecture-focused reviewer, rather than spending equal effort on architectural analysis that a second reviewer was likely to cover anyway.
125: 
126: **Fix**: when running parallel reviews deliberately, tell each reviewer that a parallel review is happening, without revealing its content. This lets reviewers self-select toward complementary strengths (e.g., "you have live web search — lean into verifying specific technical claims rather than re-deriving architecture from first principles that a parallel review will also derive") instead of duplicating effort blind.
127: 
128: ---
129: 
130: ## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS — SUMMARY FOR PROTOCOL UPDATE
131: 
132: 1. **Keep running parallel independent reviews for architecture-level decisions.** The convergence in §2 is real signal, not noise, and it was only available because the reviews were genuinely independent (§1). Don't collapse this into a single-reviewer process to save time — the two asymmetric-catch sets in §4 show real value was added on both sides that a single review would have missed on one side or the other.
133: 2. **Fix context-pack manifest accuracy before shipping to reviewers** — verify a bundle's stated purpose against its actual content (§5.1). This is a process bug with a cheap fix and an expensive failure mode if it recurs with a reviewer less inclined to double-check.
134: 3. **Keep the rigid required-sections + explicit verification-criteria template** for review requests (§5.2) — it's why this synthesis was tractable at all.
135: 4. **Add an explicit "verify current library/API status via search" instruction** to review requests touching specific technology choices (§5.3) — don't leave this to individual reviewer judgment.
136: 5. **Make cross-review synthesis a defined third stage**, not an ad hoc follow-up request (§5.4). This report is the template; formalize it.
137: 6. **Tell parallel reviewers a parallel review exists** (without sharing content) so they can lean into complementary strengths rather than duplicate effort (§5.5).
138: 
139: ---
140: 
141: ## 7. L3 PRINCIPLE (for `proposed_lessons.yaml`, per Mandate 11)
142: 
143: **L3-Parallel-Review-Convergence-Is-Signal-Divergence-Is-Direction** — When two independently-reasoning reviewers converge on a conclusion without access to each other's work, that convergence is stronger evidence than either review alone and further scrutiny should move on. When they diverge, the divergence usually points to either (a) a genuine unresolved design question worth a human decision, or (b) a source-material gap where multiple valid precedents exist and nothing adjudicates between them — distinguish which, because the fix differs (decide vs. clarify the source material). The value of running two reviews isn't redundancy — it's that architectural reasoning and empirical verification are different cognitive modes that different reviewers (or the same reviewer with different tool access) will apply unevenly, and only a synthesis pass surfaces which mode each side under-applied.
144: 
145: ---

272:         self.profile = profile
273:         self.config = self._load_profile_config(profile)
274:     
275:     def _load_profile_config(self, profile: PlatformProfile) -> dict:
276:         # Load from packer-config.yaml profiles section
277:         pass

294: 
295: ### 2. Format Adapters
296: 
297: ```python
298: class FormatAdapter(ABC):
299:     @abstractmethod
300:     def render_bundle(self, content: str, metadata: dict) -> str:
301:         pass
302:     
303:     @abstractmethod
304:     def render_manifest(self, bundles: list, metadata: dict) -> str:
305:         pass
306: 
307: class XMLFormatAdapter(FormatAdapter):
308:     """Claude-native XML with spotlighting delimiters"""
309:     def render_bundle(self, content: str, metadata: dict) -> str:
310:         # Escape content, wrap in <bundle> tags with metadata attributes
311:         escaped = self._escape_xml(content)
312:         attrs = " ".join(f'{k}="{v}"' for k, v in metadata.items())
313:         return f'<bundle {attrs}>\n{escaped}\n</bundle>'
314: 
315: class XMLMarkdownHybridAdapter(FormatAdapter):
316:     """Grok: XML structure with Markdown content"""
317:     def render_bundle(self, content: str, metadata: dict) -> str:
318:         # XML wrapper, Markdown content preserved
319:         escaped = self._escape_xml(content)  # Still escape for safety
320:         return f'<bundle format="markdown" {attrs}>\n{escaped}\n</bundle>'
321: 
322: class MarkdownStructuredAdapter(FormatAdapter):
323:     """Gemini: Markdown with structured frontmatter"""
324:     def render_bundle(self, content: str, metadata: dict) -> str:
325:         frontmatter = yaml.dump(metadata)
326:         return f"---\n{frontmatter}---\n\n{content}"
327: 
328: class MarkdownSourcesAdapter(FormatAdapter):
329:     """NotebookLM: Individual source files with citation metadata"""
330:     def render_bundle(self, content: str, metadata: dict) -> str:
331:         # Each bundle becomes a separate source file
332:         # Include NotebookLM citation markers [^1], [^2]
333:         return self._add_citation_markers(content, metadata)
334: ```
335: 
336: ### 3. Bundle Ordering Strategies
337: 
338: ```python
339: class BundleOrderingStrategy(ABC):
340:     @abstractmethod
341:     def order(self, bundles: list[Bundle], config: dict) -> list[Bundle]:
342:         pass
343: 
344: class LITMUShapedStrategy(BundleOrderingStrategy):
345:     """Claude: Critical at start/end, reference in middle"""
346:     def order(self, bundles: list[Bundle], config: dict) -> list[Bundle]:
347:         critical = [b for b in bundles if b.priority == "critical"]
348:         middle = [b for b in bundles if b.priority == "reference"]
349:         action = [b for b in bundles if b.priority == "action"]
350:         # Sort each by token count descending
351:         return (sorted(critical, key=lambda b: -b.tokens) + 
352:                 sorted(middle, key=lambda b: -b.tokens) + 
353:                 sorted(action, key=lambda b: -b.tokens))
354: 
355: class PriorityWeightedStrategy(BundleOrderingStrategy):
356:     """Grok: Weight by priority, less strict position constraints"""
357:     def order(self, bundles: list[Bundle], config: dict) -> list[Bundle]:
358:         return sorted(bundles, key=lambda b: (-b.priority_weight, -b.tokens))
359: 
360: class RelevanceDescendingStrategy(BundleOrderingStrategy):
361:     """Gemini: Most relevant first (works with retrieval)"""
362:     def order(self, bundles: list[Bundle], config: dict) -> list[Bundle]:
363:         return sorted(bundles, key=lambda b: (-b.relevance_score, -b.tokens))
364: 
365: class HierarchicalStrategy(BundleOrderingStrategy):
366:     """Gemini 3.1 Pro: Hierarchical (overview → detail → appendix)"""
367:     def order(self, bundles: list[Bundle], config: dict) -> list[Bundle]:
368:         hierarchy = {"overview": 0, "detail": 1, "appendix": 2}
369:         return sorted(bundles, key=lambda b: (hierarchy.get(b.tier, 1), -b.tokens))
370: 
371: class ThematicStrategy(BundleOrderingStrategy):
372:     """NotebookLM: Group by theme, each theme self-contained"""
373:     def order(self, bundles: list[Bundle], config: dict) -> list[Bundle]:
374:         themes = defaultdict(list)
375:         for b in bundles:
376:             themes[b.theme].append(b)
377:         # Order themes by importance, bundles within theme by relevance
378:         ordered = []
379:         for theme in sorted(themes.keys(), key=lambda t: -themes[t][0].importance):
380:             ordered.extend(sorted(themes[theme], key=lambda b: -b.relevance))
381:         return ordered
382: ```

75: ## 2. THE SCHEMA (T0a — Engine + Schema)
76: 
77: ### 2.1 File Format: YAML Frontmatter + Markdown Body
78: 
79: Follow the `structured-madr` precedent validated in `grounding_part1.xml` §1: each decision is a single `.md` file, YAML frontmatter between `---` fences, free-text rationale/narrative below.
80: 
81: ```markdown
82: ---
83: schema_version: "1.0.0"
84: id: D0001
85: title: "Use sqlite-vec for unified session-state WAL"
86: type: adr
87: category: architecture
88: status: proposed
89: tags: [database, persistence, wal]
90: created: "2026-07-19"
91: updated: "2026-07-19"
92: proposer: kali
93: authority: human
94: drivers:
95:   primary: "Need a single durable store for handoffs, gnosis, lessons, checkpoints"
96:   secondary: ["Reduce write-path complexity", "Reuse existing sqlite-vec adapter"]
97: options:
98:   - id: sqlite_vec_unified
99:     label: "Single sqlite-vec WAL database"
100:     risk_assessment: { technical: low, schedule: low, ecosystem: low }
101:     consequences:
102:       positive: ["Single writer simplifies durability", "Reuses D-282 PRAGMA SSOT"]
103:       negative: ["Write serialization bottleneck at N concurrent agents"]
104:       neutral: ["Requires partition_key per entity"]
105:   - id: per_domain_files
106:     label: "Keep per-domain JSON files (status quo)"
107:     risk_assessment: { technical: low, schedule: low, ecosystem: medium }
108:     consequences:
109:       positive: ["No migration needed"]
110:       negative: ["No cross-domain query, split-brain risk"]
111:       neutral: []
112: chosen_option: null
113: decided_at: null
114: decided_by: null
115: rationale: null
116: decision_by: "2026-08-01"
117: supersedes: null
118: superseded_by: null
119: relationships:
120:   - type: blocks
121:     target: D0010
122:   - type: depends_on
123:     target: D0002
124: meditate_scaffold_ready: true
125: slot_ref: P2
126: evidence_refs:
127:   - "grounding_part2.xml#P2-BRIGID"
128:   - "research.xml#structured-madr"
129: ---
130: 
131: ## Context
132: 
133: Free-text narrative. This is where the human/agent writes the reasoning that doesn't
134: fit structured fields. Not validated by JSON Schema — validated only for presence
135: (non-empty) if `status != proposed`.
136: 
137: ## Notes
138: 
139: Anything else.
140: ```
141: 
142: **Why frontmatter + body, not pure YAML**: Pure-YAML decision files lose the ability to hold rich prose rationale without awkward multi-line YAML block scalars, and every ADR precedent surveyed (`adr-tools`, `structured-madr`, MADR) uses this exact split. Parse with `python-frontmatter` (`pip install python-frontmatter`) since it round-trips cleanly and handles edge cases (BOM, CRLF) that a manual `str.split('---', 2)` will not.
143: 
144: **Note for builders**: Grok CLI's review independently proposed pure YAML (`docs/decisions/catalog/D001.yaml`, no frontmatter split, no markdown body) instead. Both are defensible — pure YAML is simpler to parse and matches the project's existing config-file culture (`entities.yaml`, `lenses.yaml`); frontmatter+body matches the actual ADR tooling the research cites as precedent, and gives free-text rationale a natural home instead of forcing it into a YAML block scalar. **This spec's recommendation stands (frontmatter + `.md`)** because it's what the cited precedent actually does, but if the implementing agent finds `python-frontmatter` adds friction, switching to pure `.yaml` with a `body: |` block-scalar field is a same-day, low-risk substitution — it does not change the schema's field semantics, only the file's outer envelope. Pick one before T0a starts; don't let both formats coexist in the catalog.
145: 
146: ### 2.2 Fields — What Changed from the Original Draft, Field by Field
147: 
148: | Field | Status | Note |
149: |---|---|---|
150: | `schema_version` | **NEW — required** | String, semver. Every decision file declares which schema version it was written against. Without this, you cannot safely migrate the format later. Bump this file's version in lockstep with `decision_schema.json`. |
151: | `id` | keep | Pattern `^D[0-9]{4}$`. Zero-padded to 4 digits from the start — 23 decisions today, but don't hardcode a 2-digit assumption. |
152: | `title`, `created`, `updated` | keep | `created`/`updated` are ISO 8601 dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`), not datetimes — this project's own docs use date-only stamps throughout. |
153: | `type`, `category`, `tags` | keep | `type` is a fixed const `"adr"` for now (future-proofs against non-ADR decision types later). |
154: | `status` | keep, enum extended | `proposed \| deliberating \| accepted \| superseded \| deprecated`. Added `deliberating` because MEDITATE T1-scaffold needs a state to mark "a `meditate` prompt has been rendered for this decision" distinct from `proposed`. |
155: | `authority` | keep | `human \| agent \| human_review`. Flat enum only — do **not** implement the full MAD-framework role structure (proposer/deliberator/decider/auditor) from the original doc's "Correction 6." That's T2 scope; building it now is scope creep the 9–11h budget cannot absorb. |
156: | `criteria` (weighted scoring) | **REMOVED from required schema** | Make this an optional, freeform `object` with no enforced sub-schema. Do not validate weights sum to 1.0, do not enforce a fixed criteria vocabulary. If nobody uses it, it costs nothing; if the schema enforces it, it becomes exactly the kind of stale, unmaintained ceremony that `grounding_part1.xml` Source 7 ("ADRs go stale") warns against. |
157: | `options[]` | keep, required if `status != proposed` is not enforced (options can be empty for early proposals) | `risk_assessment` and `consequences` sub-objects unchanged from the original draft — this part was already well-designed and matches `structured-madr` directly. |
158: | `chosen_option` | **NEW** | Nullable string, must match one of `options[].id`. Required non-null when `status == accepted`. This was missing from the original schema — without it, nothing records *which* option won. |
159: | `decided_at` | **NEW** | Nullable ISO date. Required non-null when `status in (accepted, deprecated)`. |
160: | `decided_by` | **NEW — [Grok catch]** | Nullable string, `agent_id` or `"human"`. Distinct from `proposer`: `proposer` is who *wrote the decision file*, `decided_by` is who *executed the accept*. These are frequently different agents in a 12+-agent fleet and collapsing them into one field loses provenance. |
161: | `rationale` | **NEW — [Grok catch]** | Nullable short string (not the full markdown body). A one-line "why this option won" that's cheap to scan in `list`/`show` output without opening the full narrative section. Required non-null when `status == accepted`. |
162: | `relationships[]` | keep | `type` enum: `blocks \| blocked_by \| supersedes \| complements \| depends_on`. |
163: | `supersedes` / `superseded_by` | **PROMOTED to top-level scalar fields**, in addition to appearing in `relationships[]` if desired | Nullable `D####` string. This is the one structural change from the original draft that matters most for CLI performance: `show D0024` needs O(1) access to walk the chain back to D0001, not a linear scan of a `relationships` array. Keep them redundant with `relationships[]` entries of type `supersedes`/`superseded_by` for graph rendering, but the CLI's chain-walk reads the scalar fields. |
164: | `meditate_scaffold_ready` | renamed from `meditate_ready` | Boolean. Renamed for clarity — this only means "a static MEDITATE prompt template can be rendered," not "MEDITATE has run" or "a verdict exists." |
165: | `slot_ref` | **replaces `persona_parameters` entirely** | Single nullable enum value: `GRAND_OVERSIGHT \| LIGHT_OVERSOUL \| DARK_OVERSOUL \| P1 \| P2 \| ... \| P10`. This is the M2-compliant replacement — see §5. |
166: | `persona_parameters` | **DELETED** | Do not implement this field in the engine schema. If T1-scaffold needs per-slot framing, it comes from the WAD overlay file (§5), never from the decision file itself. |
167: | `evidence_refs` | **NEW** | Array of strings, freeform (`"bundle_name.xml#section"` convention recommended but not enforced). Lets a decision point back at the research that justified it — matches the citation discipline already used throughout this project's own docs. |
168: | `proposer` | **NEW** | String, agent/entity name that created the file. Free text, not validated against a WAD entity list (that would itself be an M2 coupling — the engine schema shouldn't need to know what entities exist in any given WAD). |
169: | `decision_by` | keep | Nullable ISO date. **Display-only** in T0/T1 — see §6, no enforcement daemon. |
170: 
171: ### 2.3 JSON Schema Meta-Rules
172: 
173: - Use **Draft 2020-12** (`jsonschema.Draft202012Validator`, package `jsonschema`, current on PyPI). Declare `"$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema"` at the top of `decision_schema.json` explicitly — don't rely on the library's default-draft fallback, since an unpinned `$schema` means a future `jsonschema` upgrade could silently change which draft rules apply to your validation.
174: - Set `"additionalProperties": false` at the top level and on every nested object (`options[]` items, `consequences`, `risk_assessment`, `relationships[]` items). This is the "forbid-unknown" requirement from the review brief — it's what catches a typo'd field name (`autority` vs `authority`) at validation time instead of silently ignoring it forever.
175: - `required` at top level: `["schema_version", "id", "title", "status", "created", "authority"]`. Everything else is conditionally required via `if/then` (JSON Schema 2020-12 supports this natively):
176: 
177: ```json
178: {
179:   "if": { "properties": { "status": { "const": "accepted" } } },
180:   "then": { "required": ["chosen_option", "decided_at", "decided_by", "rationale"] }
181: }
182: ```
183: 
184: - Validate the schema file itself in CI: `Draft202012Validator.check_schema(json.load(open("decision_schema.json")))`. This catches a malformed schema before it silently stops validating anything.

188: ## 3. THE DECISIONENGINE CLASS (T0a)
189: 
190: ### 3.1 Location and Shape
191: 
192: `src/omega/governance/decisions.py`. A plain class, not a singleton, not a WAD-aware service — it takes a `catalog_dir: Path` in its constructor and knows nothing about entities, WADs, or slots beyond the `slot_ref` string it validates against the fixed `Slot` enum already defined in `src/omega/governance/slots.py`.
193: 
194: ```python
195: import json
196: import anyio
197: import frontmatter          # pip install python-frontmatter
198: import portalocker          # pip install portalocker>=3.2
199: from pathlib import Path
200: from jsonschema import Draft202012Validator
201: from omega.governance.slots import Slot
202: 
203: class DecisionValidationError(Exception):
204:     """Typed error per Mandate 9 (Error Integrity) — never raise bare ValueError."""
205: 
206: class DecisionNotFoundError(Exception):
207:     pass
208: 
209: class DecisionEngine:
210:     def __init__(self, catalog_dir: Path, schema_path: Path):
211:         self.catalog_dir = catalog_dir
212:         self.locks_dir = catalog_dir / ".locks"
213:         self.locks_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
214:         schema = json.loads(schema_path.read_text())
215:         Draft202012Validator.check_schema(schema)   # fail fast if schema itself is broken
216:         self._validator = Draft202012Validator(schema)
217: 
218:     async def read(self, decision_id: str) -> "Decision": ...
219:     async def list(self, status: str | None = None, tag: str | None = None) -> list["Decision"]: ...
220:     async def create(self, fields: dict, body: str) -> "Decision": ...
221:     async def decide(self, decision_id: str, option_id: str, human_confirmed: bool) -> "Decision": ...
222:     def _validate(self, fields: dict) -> None: ...
223:     def _atomic_write(self, path: Path, content: bytes) -> None: ...
224:     def _allocate_id(self) -> str: ...
225:     def _actor_id(self) -> str: ...
226:     def _today(self) -> str: ...
227:     def _path_for(self, decision_id: str) -> Path: ...
228:     def _read_sync(self, decision_id: str) -> "Decision": ...
229:     def _serialize(self, fields: dict, body: str) -> bytes: ...
230: ```
231: 
232: ### 3.2 Atomic Writes — Exact Pattern to Use
233: 
234: `atomicwrites` (the PyPI package once suggested for this kind of thing) was **archived by its upstream author in 2022** and formally deprecated from downstream package repositories in 2025, with upstream's own guidance being "use `os.replace`/`os.rename` instead." **Do not add `atomicwrites` as a dependency.** Roll the four-line pattern yourself:
235: 
236: ```python
237: import os
238: import tempfile
239: 
240: def _atomic_write(self, path: Path, content: bytes) -> None:
241:     fd, tmp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(
242:         dir=path.parent,          # MUST be same directory as target — same filesystem is required for os.replace to be atomic
243:         prefix=f".{path.name}.",
244:         suffix=".tmp",
245:     )
246:     try:
247:         with os.fdopen(fd, "wb") as f:
248:             f.write(content)
249:             f.flush()
250:             os.fsync(f.fileno())   # forces kernel to write to disk before the rename is visible
251:         os.replace(tmp_path, path)  # atomic on POSIX; MoveFileEx-based on Windows via os.replace's ctypes fallback
252:     except Exception:
253:         os.unlink(tmp_path)        # clean up the temp file if anything above failed
254:         raise
255: ```
256: 
257: Three things that matter and are easy to get wrong:
258: 1. **The temp file must be created in the same directory as the target**, not `/tmp` — `os.replace` is only atomic when source and destination are on the same filesystem, and a container's `/tmp` may be a different mount than `docs/decisions/catalog/`.
259: 2. **Call `f.flush()` then `os.fsync(f.fileno())` before `os.replace`** — without the fsync, the rename can complete while the actual file content is still sitting in a kernel buffer, so a crash between rename and buffer-flush can leave you with a zero-length or truncated file even though the rename itself succeeded.
260: 3. Because this is Mandate-1 (AnyIO Absolute) territory, wrap the actual call site in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync(self._atomic_write, path, content)` from the `async def create()`/`decide()` methods — `_atomic_write` itself stays a plain synchronous function (blocking file I/O has no business being `async def`), and AnyIO pushes it off the event loop.
261: 
262: ### 3.3 Locking — Exact Library and Pattern to Use
263: 
264: Do not hand-roll `fcntl`/`msvcrt` branching. Use **`portalocker`** (`pip install portalocker`, current major version 3.x, actively maintained, explicitly cross-platform for Windows/Linux/BSD/macOS — unlike raw `fcntl` which is POSIX-only and would silently break if this ever runs on a contributor's Windows machine). Portalocker's `Lock` context manager takes a `timeout` directly, which gives you a clean way to fail fast instead of hanging:
265: 
266: ```python
267: async def decide(self, decision_id: str, option_id: str, human_confirmed: bool) -> "Decision":
268:     decision = await self.read(decision_id)
269:     if decision.authority == "human" and not human_confirmed:
270:         raise DecisionValidationError(f"{decision_id} requires --human-confirmed")
271: 
272:     lock_path = self.locks_dir / f"{decision_id}.lock"
273: 
274:     def _do_decide():
275:         with portalocker.Lock(str(lock_path), timeout=5, mode="w") as _:
276:             # re-read inside the lock — another agent may have superseded it
277:             # while we were waiting for the lock
278:             current = self._read_sync(decision_id)
279:             # [Grok catch] Idempotency: decide() is only valid on a HEAD-of-chain
280:             # record. Reject anything that isn't proposed/deliberating explicitly
281:             # — don't just special-case "superseded". An already-accepted decision
282:             # must be re-opened via an explicit new supersession, not silently
283:             # re-decided, or you get two "accepted" records for one question.
284:             if current.status not in ("proposed", "deliberating"):
285:                 raise DecisionValidationError(
286:                     f"{decision_id} has status={current.status!r}; decide() only "
287:                     f"operates on proposed/deliberating records. To change an "
288:                     f"accepted decision, supersede its current head instead."
289:                 )
290:             if option_id not in {o["id"] for o in current.fields.get("options", [])}:
291:                 raise DecisionValidationError(f"option {option_id!r} not found in {decision_id}.options")
292:             new_id = self._allocate_id()   # see id-allocation note below — locked separately
293:             new_fields = {**current.fields, "id": new_id, "supersedes": decision_id,
294:                           "status": "accepted", "chosen_option": option_id,
295:                           "decided_by": self._actor_id(), "decided_at": self._today()}
296:             self._atomic_write(self._path_for(new_id), self._serialize(new_fields, ""))
297:             updated_current = {**current.fields, "status": "superseded", "superseded_by": new_id}
298:             self._atomic_write(self._path_for(decision_id), self._serialize(updated_current, current.body))
299:             return new_id
300: 
301:     new_id = await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(_do_decide)
302:     return await self.read(new_id)
303: ```
304: 
305: **Re-read inside the lock, not before it.** This is the one concurrency bug that will actually happen with 12+ agents in the fleet (`engine_state.xml` §2): agent A reads D0001 as `proposed`, agent B acquires the lock first and supersedes it to D0024, then agent A acquires the lock and — if it trusted its stale pre-lock read — would supersede an already-superseded decision, creating two competing successors. The fix is cheap: re-read the file *after* acquiring the lock, immediately before mutating.
306: 
307: **ID allocation has its own race condition — separate from the per-decision lock above.** `_allocate_id()` (reading the catalog directory for the current max `D####` and returning max+1) must **not** just scan the directory unlocked: two agents calling `decide()` on two *different* source decisions at the same moment can both scan the catalog, both see the same max id, and both write `D0025`, silently clobbering one of them via `os.replace`. Guard allocation with its own lock file, separate from the per-decision locks, e.g. `docs/decisions/catalog/.locks/_id_allocator.lock`, and hold it only for the scan-and-reserve step (not the whole `decide()` call):
308: 
309: ```python
310: def _allocate_id(self) -> str:
311:     alloc_lock = self.locks_dir / "_id_allocator.lock"
312:     with portalocker.Lock(str(alloc_lock), timeout=5, mode="w"):
313:         existing = [int(p.stem[1:]) for p in self.catalog_dir.glob("D[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9].*")]
314:         next_n = (max(existing) if existing else 0) + 1
315:         return f"D{next_n:04d}"
316: ```
317: 
318: This is cheap (a directory glob + a lock acquire/release, not a full write), and it's the difference between "23 decisions" and "23 decisions, one of which silently vanished because two agents raced the allocator." Write a contract test for this specifically: spawn two concurrent `decide()` calls on two different source decisions and assert both successor ids are distinct and both files exist.
319: 
320: ### 3.4 Supersession Is the Only Mutation Path
321: 
322: Never open an existing decision file and rewrite fields in place except for the two specific, narrow cases above: (a) `status: proposed → superseded` + setting `superseded_by`, and (b) creating the new successor file. Every other field change — editing a typo in `title`, adding an `evidence_refs` entry — should also go through `decide`-style supersession once a decision has left `status: proposed`. While `status == proposed`, direct in-place edits (still via `_atomic_write`, still through the lock) are fine, since nothing has been decided yet and there's nothing to preserve immutably.
323: 
324: ---

326: ## 4. CLI (T1-core + T1-graph)
327: 
328: ### 4.1 Typer Wiring
329: 
330: Follow the exact pattern the project's own `oracle_cli.py` already uses (per `engine_state.xml` §3, "Typer CLI"). Register as a sub-Typer, not a flat top-level command list:
331: 
332: ```python

335: decision_app = typer.Typer(help="Manage decision records")

341:     tag: str = typer.Option(None, help="Filter by tag"),
342:     overdue: bool = typer.Option(False, "--overdue", help="Filter to decision_by < today AND status == proposed"),
343:     meditate_ready: bool = typer.Option(False, "--meditate-ready", help="Filter to meditate_scaffold_ready: true"),
344:     json_out: bool = typer.Option(False, "--json", help="Emit machine-readable JSON"),
345: ): ...
346: 
347: @decision_app.command("show")

349: 
350: @decision_app.command("decide")

352:     decision_id: str,
353:     option: str = typer.Option(..., "--option"),
354:     human_confirmed: bool = typer.Option(False, "--human-confirmed"),
355: ): ...
356: 
357: @decision_app.command("validate")
358: def validate_decisions(
359:     decision_id: str = typer.Argument(None, help="Specific decision to validate, or all if omitted"),
360:     json_out: bool = typer.Option(False, "--json"),
361: ): ...
362: 
363: @decision_app.command("graph")
364: def graph_decisions(
365:     focus: str = typer.Option(None, "--focus"),
366:     depth: int = typer.Option(2, "--depth"),
367:     color: bool = typer.Option(False, "--color"),
368: ): ...
369: 
370: # src/omega/cli/oracle_cli.py  (wherever the root Typer app is assembled)
371: from omega.cli.decision_cli import decision_app
372: app.add_typer(decision_app, name="decision")
373: ```
374: 
375: This gives you `omega decision list`, `omega decision show D0001`, etc. for free — no custom argument-parsing needed, and it matches the existing `app.add_typer(sub.app, name="...")` idiom the project already uses elsewhere for `db`/`items`-style command groups.
376: 
377: ### 4.2 Command-by-Command Spec
378: 
379: **`omega decision list [--tier PX] [--status S] [--tag T] [--overdue] [--meditate-ready] [--json]`**  
380: Default output: a plain table (id, title, status, slot_ref, decision_by). `--json` emits an array of full decision objects. Exit code 0 always (empty result is not an error — print "No decisions match." to stderr, empty array to stdout if `--json`). `--overdue` (**[Grok catch]**) filters to `decision_by < today AND status == proposed` — this is the cheap, correct substitute for a deadline-enforcement daemon: same information, no background process, no Hivemind alert plumbing to build and maintain. `--meditate-ready` filters to `meditate_scaffold_ready: true`, useful for an agent scanning "what's ready for a MEDITATE pass."
381: 
382: **`omega decision validate [--all | DECISION_ID]`** — **[Grok catch, add this]**  
383: Runs the JSON Schema over one decision or the whole catalog and reports pass/fail per file, without mutating anything. This is a ~30-minute addition on top of the validator you already built for `create`/`decide`, and it's the single highest-ROI command for T0b migration: run `omega decision validate --all` after every migration batch instead of discovering a malformed file only when `list`/`show` chokes on it later. Exit code 0 if all pass, 1 if any fail (with per-file error detail to stderr).
384: 
385: **`omega decision show D0001 [--json]`**  
386: Prints the full decision, including a rendered supersession chain if `supersedes`/`superseded_by` is non-null: `D0001 (superseded) → D0024 (accepted)`. Walks the scalar fields (§2.2), not the `relationships[]` array. Exit code 1 if the id doesn't exist, with a message to stderr — never print a Python traceback to a human-facing CLI.
387: 
388: **`omega decision decide D0001 --option amend [--human-confirmed]`**  
389: Per §3.3. If `authority: human` and `--human-confirmed` is absent, exit code 2 (distinct from the "not found" exit code 1, so scripts/handoffs can distinguish "you didn't confirm" from "the id is wrong") with a clear stderr message. On success, print the new decision's id to stdout (so it can be captured: `NEW_ID=$(omega decision decide D0001 --option amend --human-confirmed)`).
390: 
391: **`omega decision graph [--focus D0001] [--depth 2] [--color]`**  
392: Renders all five relationship types (`blocks`, `blocked_by`, `supersedes`, `complements`, `depends_on`) as ASCII, not just blocking edges — this was explicit in the original spec's Correction 4 and is worth keeping. Plain ASCII by default (per the review: this output gets embedded in Hivemind handoff packets and CI logs, where ANSI color codes just show up as garbage `\x1b[...]` sequences). `--color` opts into ANSI for interactive terminal use. **Detect cycles before rendering** (`depends_on`/`blocks` edges that loop back on themselves via a hand-authored decision file are a real possibility once >20 files exist) — a plain DFS visited-set check is enough; on detection, print the cycle path to stderr and exit non-zero rather than looping forever or silently truncating the graph.
393: 
394: ### 4.3 Exit Codes (Contract, Not Suggestion)
395: 
396: Agents and CI scripts branch on these — treat them as part of the API, not an afterthought:
397: 
398: | Code | Meaning | Commands |
399: |---|---|---|
400: | `0` | Success (including "list returned zero rows") | all |
401: | `1` | Decision id not found, or `validate` found ≥1 schema failure | `show`, `decide`, `validate` |
402: | `2` | `authority: human` decision missing `--human-confirmed` | `decide` |
403: | `3` | Schema/engine failure — malformed `decision_schema.json` itself, lock timeout, or attempted `decide` on a non-`proposed`/`deliberating` record (§3.4 idempotency fix) | `decide`, engine startup |
404: 
405: Never let an unhandled Python exception surface as a raw traceback to stdout/stderr in the CLI layer — catch `DecisionValidationError`/`DecisionNotFoundError` at the Typer command boundary and map to the codes above (this is also Mandate 9, Error Integrity, in practice, not just UX polish).
406: 
407: ### 4.4 What NOT to Build in T1
408: 
409: - No `--watch` / live-reload mode.
410: - No deadline-enforcement daemon reading `decision_by` and firing alerts — `decision_by` is a **read-only "days remaining" column** in `list`/`show` output for T0/T1, nothing more. A real enforcer belongs with the Anubis TTL-enforcer pattern already scoped as its own phase in `grounding_part2.xml` P9 — don't duplicate that infrastructure inside the decision CLI.
411: - No interactive `decide` wizard (prompt-driven option selection). Flags only for T1; a TUI wizard is a T2+ nicety.
412: 
413: ---
414: 
415: ## 5. MEDITATE T1-SCAFFOLD (Static Template Only — No BE Math)
416: 
417: ### 5.1 Why the Original Design Doesn't Work as Specified
418: 
419: The Belief Engine paper (`arXiv:2605.15343v1`, verified in `grounding_part2.xml`) validates numeric `uptake`/`anchoring` parameters inside an **iterative, multi-turn belief-update loop**: extract arguments → judge evidence → update structured memory → update belief state (this is where the log-odds math with `u`/`a` actually executes) → compose response. Omega's MEDITATE, by the project's own architecture (`grounding_part1.xml`'s Belief-Engine-to-MEDITATE mapping table), is a **single-inference, sequential persona immersion inside one oracle call**. There is no loop in which a numeric float gets iteratively applied. Handing the model a JSON blob of `{uptake: 0.4, anchoring: 0.7}` in a single-shot prompt doesn't invoke belief-engine math — it's a number the model reads once and can only use as a vague qualitative hint, which is what a plain adjective would have done just as well, without borrowing false rigor from a paper whose actual mechanism isn't present.
420: 
421: ### 5.2 What T1-Scaffold Actually Builds
422: 
423: A static Jinja2 (or plain f-string, no need for a templating engine at this scale) prompt template that:
424: 
425: 1. Reads `slot_ref` from the decision file.
426: 2. Looks up that slot in the **active WAD's** `config/wads/<iwad>/decisions/slot_overlay.yaml` — not in the decision file itself — to get a qualitative stance descriptor and (for a PWAD like `arcana_novai`) a display name.
427: 3. Renders the decision's title, drivers, options, and consequences into a prompt, with the slot's qualitative framing prepended.
428: 4. Prints the rendered prompt to stdout (or writes it to a file) for a human/agent to paste into an actual MEDITATE session. **T1-scaffold does not call the oracle. It does not run inference.** That's explicitly deferred — building the auto-invocation now means building against an integration point (`Oracle.talk()`/`summon()`) that isn't part of this review's scope and risks scope-creeping a 1h task into a multi-day one.
429: 
430: `config/wads/_omega_default/decisions/slot_overlay.yaml` (IWAD default — engine-native, no mythic names):
431: ```yaml
432: P1: { stance: "anchored in infrastructure reality, evidence-responsive on deployment risk" }
433: P2: { stance: "anchored on data-integrity concerns, receptive to durability evidence" }
434: # ... P3-P10, LIGHT_OVERSOUL, DARK_OVERSOUL, GRAND_OVERSIGHT
435: ```
436: 
437: `config/wads/arcana_novai/decisions/slot_overlay.yaml` (PWAD overlay — mythic names live HERE, never in engine code):
438: ```yaml
439: P1: { display_name: "Sekhmet", stance: "anchored in infrastructure reality, evidence-responsive on deployment risk" }
440: P2: { display_name: "Brigid", stance: "anchored on data-integrity concerns, receptive to durability evidence" }
441: # ...
442: ```
443: 
444: This is the direct, correct application of the M2 pattern already proven in `HMC_QUAD_FORGE_IMPLEMENTATION_MANUAL_20260718.md` §3 for meditate lenses generally (`_omega_default/meditate/lenses.yaml` base + `arcana_novai/meditate/overlay.yaml` mapping) — decision-tools T1-scaffold should reuse that exact base+overlay resolution mechanism, not invent a parallel one.
445: 
446: ### 5.3 Deferred to T2 (Do Not Build Now)
447: 
448: Full Belief-Engine-parameterized iterative deliberation, automatic oracle invocation, and verdict extraction back into `chosen_option`. T2 is already gated in the original doc behind "decision count > 50 or stalled > 2 weeks" — leave it there.
449: 
450: ---
451: 
452: ## 6. MIGRATION (T0b)
453: 
454: ### 6.1 Two-PR Strategy — Do Not Combine
455: 
456: **PR 1**: `DecisionEngine` + `decision_schema.json` + CLI + tests, with **zero decision files migrated**. Merge this first, fully tested, fully gated by `make decision-schema-check` (§7), before touching a single one of the 23 existing decisions.
457: 
458: **PR 2**: Migration of the 23 decisions currently described in prose across `engine_state.xml`, `implementation.xml` (`SOVEREIGN_ARK_BLUEPRINT.md`), and `PIVOT_LOG.md` into the new format.
459: 
460: Reasons to split, not bundle: (1) PR 1 is independently testable and revertable without touching content; (2) migrating 23 real decisions surfaces schema gaps (a decision that doesn't cleanly fit `options[]`, a status that doesn't map cleanly to the five-value enum) that are much cheaper to fix *before* the schema is locked than after; (3) it matches the "build from pain, not speculation" principle the source docs already invoke — don't guess what the schema needs to hold before you've tried pouring the real data in.
461: 
462: ### 6.2 Migration Mechanics
463: 
464: - During PR 2, set `"additionalProperties": true` temporarily on the schema (or run a `--lenient` validation mode) so imperfect first-pass migrations don't block on cosmetic mismatches. Tighten back to `false` once all 23 decisions validate cleanly under the strict schema, as a final step of PR 2 before merge.
465: - Every migrated decision gets `evidence_refs` pointing back at the source document it was extracted from (e.g., `evidence_refs: ["engine_state.xml#section-D-298"]`) — this preserves the citation trail instead of losing it in the migration.
466: - Do not hand-write all 23 by hand from scratch. Write one small one-off script (not part of the shipped `DecisionEngine` API) that parses the existing markdown tables in `engine_state.xml`/`implementation.xml` and pre-fills a first-draft frontmatter block per decision; a human/agent then reviews and fills in `options`/`consequences` where the source prose didn't already structure them clearly. Delete the one-off script after migration — it's not a maintained tool.
467: 
468: ---
469: 
470: ## 7. VALIDATION GATE (Makefile Target)
471: 
472: Add to the `Makefile`, matching the existing gate pattern (`firewall-check`, `mandate-amendment-check`, `kernel-import-check` per `engine_state.xml` §2):
473: 
474: ```makefile
475: decision-schema-check:
476: 	@echo "🔱 Decision Schema Gate"
477: 	python -c "import json; from jsonschema import Draft202012Validator; \
478: 		Draft202012Validator.check_schema(json.load(open('src/omega/governance/decision_schema.json')))"
479: 	pytest tests/test_decision_schema.py tests/test_decision_engine.py tests/test_decision_cli.py -v
480: ```
481: 
482: And wire it into `temple-grade` alongside the other gates already listed in `engine_state.xml` §2's ratified-protocol table.

484: ---
485: 
486: ## 8. CORRECTED SCHEDULE AND AGENT ASSIGNMENT
487: 
488: | Phase | Scope | Hours | Suggested Owner | Acceptance Gate | Priority |
489: |---|---|---|---|---|---|
490: | **T0a** | `decision_schema.json` + `DecisionEngine` (read/list/create/decide) + atomic writes + portalocker locking + id-allocator lock (§3.4) | 2h | Roc (established the M2-pattern template in Phase A of the HMC manual — reuse that muscle memory) | `pytest tests/test_decision_engine.py` green; concurrent-decide contract test (two threads racing `decide` on the same id) passes without producing two successors; concurrent-`decide`-on-different-ids test proves no id collision | **Definition of done — non-negotiable** |
491: | **T0b** | Migrate 23 decisions, two-PR strategy per §6, validated via `omega decision validate --all` | 2.5h | Researcher (already owns Phases B–E of the M2 migration — same "extract from prose, restructure to schema" skill) | All 23 files validate under strict schema (`additionalProperties: false`); `evidence_refs` populated for each | **Definition of done — non-negotiable** |
492: | **T1-core** | CLI `list/show/decide/validate` + supersession-chain display | 3h | Researcher or Roc (whichever finishes T0 first) | `pytest tests/test_decision_cli.py`; exit codes 0/1/2/3 verified per §4.3's table | **Definition of done — non-negotiable** |
493: | **T1-graph** | `graph` command, all 5 relationship types, plain-ASCII default, cycle detection | 0.5–1.5h (deadline enforcer explicitly cut, see §4.4 — use `list --overdue` instead) | same | Manual smoke test: 5-node graph with mixed relationship types renders without truncation; cycle test triggers non-zero exit, not a hang | **Stretch — cut first if the sprint is running long** |
494: | **T1-scaffold** | Static MEDITATE prompt template, slot-keyed, no numeric BE params | 1–2h | Whoever built the `arcana_novai/meditate/overlay.yaml` resolver in HMC Phase A (same resolution logic, new overlay file) | Rendered prompt contains zero numeric `uptake`/`anchoring` values; `grep -r "Sekhmet\|Brigid\|Prometheus" src/omega/` returns nothing | **Stretch — cut second, or push to next sprint** |
495: | **Total** | | **9h target, 9–11h realistic range** | | | |
496: 
497: **Stretch-goal framing is deliberate, not padding.** Both independent reviews (§0.1) agree T0+T1-core is the actual definition of done for this sprint; T1-graph and T1-scaffold are valuable but should not be allowed to compress T0a/T0b's quality bar to fit the clock. If the sprint is running long at the T1-core checkpoint, ship T0+T1-core alone and open T1-graph/T1-scaffold as a fast-follow — don't rush the schema/migration to make room for the graph command.
498: 
499: **Hard stop, unchanged from the original doc**: do not begin T2 (full BE verdict extraction, automatic oracle invocation) until decision count exceeds 50 or the T1 workflow has stalled for 2+ weeks. This spec only covers T0+T1.
500: 
501: ---
502: 
503: ## 9. MANDATE COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST (Verify Before Merge)
504: 
505: | Mandate | Check |
506: |---|---|
507: | **M1 AnyIO Absolute** | `grep -rn "asyncio" src/omega/governance/decisions.py src/omega/cli/decision_cli.py` returns nothing; all blocking I/O wrapped in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` |
508: | **M2 Engine-Stack Firewall** | `grep -rEn "Sekhmet\|Brigid\|Prometheus\|Saraswati\|Inanna\|Ereshkigal\|Lucifer\|Hecate\|Anubis" src/omega/` returns nothing. Mythic names exist only under `config/wads/arcana_novai/` |
509: | **M9 Error Integrity** | No bare `except:`; `DecisionValidationError`/`DecisionNotFoundError` are typed subclasses, tests cover each raise path with `pytest.raises(...)` |
510: | **M13 Temple-Grade** | `decision-schema-check` wired into `make temple-grade` |
511: | **M16 Modularization** | No hardcoded absolute paths in `decisions.py` — `catalog_dir` passed in via `config_resolver`, not literal strings |
512: | **M21 Gate Integrity** | Contract test asserts `isinstance(engine.read(...), Decision)` — not a mock returning a dict/tuple |
513: | **M23 Failure Integrity** | If `decision_schema.json` fails `check_schema()` at engine startup, raise immediately — do not silently fall back to unvalidated writes |

531: > Build T0a (schema + engine, Roc) and T0b (migration, Researcher) in parallel where possible, then T1-core is the real finish line — T1-graph/T1-scaffold are stretch, cut first if time runs short. But most creators can get significantly more mileage from their free account before upgrading makes sense.\n\n**Upgrade to Plus or Pro when:**\n\n* You're managing knowledge bases across multiple ongoing projects simultaneously\n* You're part of a team working from a shared notebook (source limits apply per collaborator)\n* You've already tried batching and consolidation and still consistently need more than 50 slots\n\n**Stay on the free tier and optimize when:**\n\n* You're focused on one content niche or vertical at a time\n* You haven't tried batching social posts yet\n* You're still working out how to use NotebookLM as a content creator\nThe NotebookLM audio overview feature and most other capabilities are available on the free plan — the source limit is often the first constraint creators hit, and it's frequently solvable without paying.\n\n## Frequently Asked Questions\n\n### How many sources can you add to NotebookLM for free?\n\nFree and Standard accounts support up to 50 sources per notebook, across up to 100 notebooks. Upgrading to NotebookLM Plus or Pro increases the per-notebook limit to 300 sources. The Ultra plan (Google's highest AI tier) allows up to 600 sources per notebook. You can also work around the limit for free by consolidating content before uploading, as described above.\n\n### Does each social post count as a separate source?\n\nYes, if you upload each post individually.\nThat's why batching social content — using [PostToSource](https://www.posttosource.com) to convert multiple links into a single grouped document — is more efficient.
